title: MSG: The Secret Ingredient?
description: UTOP 3201 Teaching Exercise 1 — a 30-minute peer-teaching tasting lesson on umami, glutamate and the difference between taste impressions and scientific claims.

slides.title: MSG: The Secret Ingredient?
slides.body: Can MSG make food taste better, and how can we tell?
slides.notes: Stage 1 (0–3 min). Lead teacher introduces the lesson and asks: “What do you expect MSG to change?” Helper explains the QR code and that responses use one word or a few words — there are no fixed answer choices. Allow scanning time.

slides.question: What do you expect MSG to change?
slides.notes: Possible responses: savoury, salty, spicy, no difference. Accept every answer — this activates prior knowledge (LO1).

slides.question: Which best describes what you already know about MSG?

options.text: I have never heard of it
I know it as a food additive
I can explain what glutamate is

slides.notes: Invite prior beliefs, then later distinguish observation from evidence. Define MSG and umami clearly before moving on.

slides.question: Which basic taste is most closely associated with glutamate?
slides.explanation: Umami is the savoury taste associated with glutamate. Saltiness is a different taste.
slides.notes: Unscored warm-up — a quick check of what learners already think.

slides.title: Before you taste
steps: Tasting is voluntary. You can observe and still answer every question.
Read the ingredient and allergen sheet first. Beef, wheat or gluten, butter (milk) and bonito (fish) may be present.
If you have an allergy or a dietary limit, do not taste. Take the observer role.
Wash your hands and use only your own cups and utensils.
Never share food that has been bitten, and never return food to a shared container.

callout.text: Not sure? Observe. You never have to taste to take part.

slides.notes: Stage 2 (3–8 min). Share ingredient labels and allergen information. Helpers distribute at least five crackers and five jerky pieces plus individual powder portions. Use a clean utensil for optional butter; apply the same thin layer to the reference and every powder piece.

slides.question: How would you like to take part in the tasting?

options.text: I will observe and describe what I see and hear

slides.notes: A silent, anonymous vote lowers the barrier to taking part. All three choices are equally welcome.

slides.title: How each round works
steps: Try the unseasoned reference piece first.
Take four fresh pieces. Dip each one once into a different powder: MSG, dried mushroom, kombu or bonito.
Single-dip rule: do not re-dip or double-dip.
Compare each piece with the reference, then answer on your phone straight away.
Unexpected impressions and “no difference” are welcome answers.

callout.text: Observers: describe what you see and hear, or watch the responses come in.

slides.notes: Demonstrate the single-dip method: take an untouched piece, dip once into one personal powder cup, eat. Do not dip again or return it to a shared cup.

slides.title: Round 1: soda crackers
slides.body: Reference first, then four powders. Answer on your phone when you are done.
slides.notes: Stage 3 (8–15 min). Start the timekeeper. Helpers monitor portions, hygiene and phone access.

slides.question: Soda crackers: in one word or a few words, what changed, if anything?
slides.notes: Do not provide a preset answer list. Display and discuss the differences learners noticed. Short explanation: MSG supplies glutamate, which is associated with umami. A savoury taste is different from a salty taste.

slides.question: Beef jerky is next. How will the difference compare with the crackers?
slides.notes: Experiment step: learners predict the second food's result, then test the prediction in the jerky round.

slides.title: Round 2: beef jerky
slides.body:
Same steps, new food: the reference piece first, then four pieces with one dip each.

Commercial jerky may already contain MSG or other flavour enhancers, which can affect the comparison.

You do not have to prefer any of the powders.
slides.notes: Stage 4 (15–22 min). Helpers monitor the single-dip method and keep track of time.

slides.question: Beef jerky: in one word or a few words, what changed, if anything?
slides.notes: Display and discuss. Compare with the cracker responses — their preferences are personal and do not prove a general claim about MSG.

slides.question: Beef jerky: how noticeable was the difference between the reference and the powder-coated pieces?
slides.notes: Observers may describe what they noticed from others, or skip this one.

slides.question: Why might the two foods respond differently?
slides.notes: Stage 5. Expect explanations based on the food itself (e.g. jerky may already contain flavour enhancers), preparation, or individual sensitivity and preference.

slides.title: What is MSG?
slides.body:
- L-glutamic acid, also called 2-aminopentanedioic acid, has a sodium salt: monosodium L-glutamate (MSG).
- Anhydrous formula of MSG: C5H8NNaO4.
- **Glutamate** is the ion responsible for the savoury taste associated with **umami**.
- The substance responsible for **salty** taste is sodium chloride, NaCl.
- Glutamate occurs naturally in tomatoes, mushrooms and kombu.

image.alt: Structural sketch of glutamate: a five-carbon chain with an amino group on the second carbon and carboxyl groups at both ends, with Na+ as the counter-ion.

slides.notes: Stage 5 (22–27 min). Show L-glutamic acid and its sodium salt, then the five-carbon structure HOOC-CH(NH2)-CH2-CH2-COO⁻ Na⁺. Explain umami versus the saltiness of NaCl using tomatoes, mushrooms and kombu as natural glutamate. The structure slide can be omitted if time is short.

slides.title: Your taste versus the evidence
slides.body:
**What we observed.** Impressions from this room. They are personal: some people notice a difference, some do not, and preferences vary.

**What science can say.** Glutamate is associated with umami; sodium chloride is responsible for saltiness.

A preference does not prove that MSG makes food taste better for everyone. For health or safety claims, look at sourced evidence, such as the U.S. FDA’s Questions and Answers on MSG.
slides.notes: Preference is subjective; the comparison tests perceived differences, not universal improvement. Do not promise that MSG will improve taste for everyone.

slides.question: Which part of monosodium glutamate (MSG) is responsible for the umami taste?
slides.explanation: Glutamate is the ion associated with the savoury taste of umami. Sodium chloride (NaCl) is what tastes salty.
slides.notes: Final knowledge check, question 1 of 3 (LO1).

slides.question: Which statement is a scientific claim rather than a personal preference?

options.text: Glutamate is associated with umami; sodium chloride is responsible for saltiness.

slides.explanation: Preferences are personal. A statement about what glutamate or NaCl does can be checked against evidence.
slides.notes: Question 2 of 3 — keeps subjective impressions and objective claims apart (LO2).

slides.question: Which foods contain glutamate naturally?
slides.explanation: Glutamate occurs naturally in many foods, including tomatoes, mushrooms and kombu.
slides.notes: Question 3 of 3. Show the leaderboard after revealing the answer.

slides.question: How confident are you that you could explain what umami is?
slides.notes: Stage 6 (27–30 min): quick confidence check before the closing reflection.

slides.question: Can MSG make food taste better, and how can we tell?
slides.notes: Return to the guiding question. Distinguish umami from saltiness and reflect on a taste difference — or on noticing no difference. Discuss without promising MSG improves taste for everyone.

slides.title: Quick feedback on this lesson
slides.description: Three short questions. Your answers help the teaching team improve.

questions.question: How clear was the explanation of umami?

slides.title: Thank you
slides.body:
Taste is personal. Evidence is shared.

**Sources**
- U.S. Food and Drug Administration, “Questions and Answers on Monosodium Glutamate (MSG)”
- NIH PubChem, monosodium glutamate compound record
- Hong Kong Centre for Food Safety, allergen guidance
- World Health Organization, Five Keys to Safer Food Manual
slides.notes: Helpers collect used cups and food safely and assist with late responses.
